en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Gabbhinīvagga 67.
The Third Training Rule Concerning a Woman in Childbirth.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, nuns were giving the full admission to a married girl who was more than twelve years old and had trained for two years in the six rules, but who had not been authorized by the Saṅgha.
The nuns said to her:
"Come, trainee; find this, give this, bring this, there is need for this, and make this allowable."
They replied, “We are not trainee nuns (sikkhamānā), noble lady; we are bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, complained, and spread it about, saying:
“How can these bhikkhunīs give the full admission to a married girl who is more than twelve years old and has trained for two years in the six rules, yet she has not been authorized by the Saṅgha?

… [The Buddha asked: “Is it true, monks, that bhikkhunīs are giving the full admission to a married girl who is more than twelve years old and has trained for two years in the six rules, even though she has not been authorized by the Saṅgha?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can these bhikkhunīs ordain a married girl who is twelve years old and has trained for two years in the six rules, yet has not been authorized by the Saṅgha?
This, monks, is neither for the pleasing of those without confidence nor for the increase of those with confidence…” [and so on].
Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to grant the formal authorization for ordination to a married woman who is full twelve years of age and has trained in the six rules for two years.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be granted in this way:
when she has been married for twelve full years, and has trained in the six rules for two years,
she should approach the Saṅgha, arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the bhikkhunīs, and squat down.
Having sat down and raised her joined palms, she should speak thus:

‘Venerable lady, I, so-and-so, who am twelve years of age and have been married, having trained for two years in the six rules under the venerable lady so-and-so, request the Saṅgha’s authorization for ordination.
She should request it a second time as well.
A third time she should be requested.
An experienced and competent bhikkhunī should inform the Saṅgha:
"Let the noble Saṅgha listen to me.

This woman, named so-and-so, who has been married for twelve full years and has trained in the six rules for two years under the noble lady named so-and-so, requests formal permission from the Saṅgha for her ordination.

If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant formal permission for the ordination of this woman, named so-and-so, who has been married for twelve full years and has trained in the six rules for two years.
This is the motion.
"Let the noble Saṅgha hear me:

This lady named so-and-so, who has been married for twelve full years and has trained in the six rules for two years under the noble lady named so-and-so, requests from the Saṅgha permission to go forth.
The Saṅgha grants permission to go forth to this lady named so-and-so, who has been married for twelve full years and has trained in the six rules for two years."

Whichever noble lady approves of granting the authorization for ordination to the woman named so-and-so, who is twelve years of age, married, and has trained for two years in the six rules, let her remain silent;
whichever does not approve, let her speak.
The Sangha has granted the authorization for ordination to the woman named so-and-so, who is twelve years of age, married, and has trained for two years in the six rules.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked those bhikkhunīs in many ways for being difficult to support … [as before] … “And furthermore, bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule:”

“Whatever nun should give the full admission to a married girl who is more than twelve years old, who has trained for two years in the six rules, but who has not been authorized by the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so on].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Having completed twelve years" means:
"Having reached twelve years.
"One who has gone to a householder" means one who has entered into another man's [keeping].
"Two years" means two full years.
"One who has trained in the training" means:

"Trained in the six rules" means that the formal authorization for her restoration has not been granted by means of a legal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
“Should give the full admission” means:
she should confer the higher ordination (*upasampadā*).

If, thinking “I will give the full admission,” she seeks out a group, a preceptor (*ācariyā*), a bowl, or a robe, or if she demarcates a boundary (*sīmā*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For each of the two formal proclamations (kammavācā), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation, the preceptor incurs an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
For the community and for the preceptor, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she gives the full admission in a legitimate legal procedure while perceiving it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If she gives the full admission in a legitimate legal procedure while being in doubt, there is an offense entailing expiation.

If it is a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*) and she perceives it as an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*), yet she causes [the person] to leave [the robe-making ceremony], there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If it is an illegitimate legal act and she perceives it as a legitimate legal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If it is an illegitimate legal act and she is uncertain about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if she ordains one who has reached twelve years of age, is married, has trained for two years in the six rules, and has been approved by the Saṅgha.
[It is] for one who is insane,
for one who is a first-time offender.
The seventh training rule is finished.
